title: Poverty, Place and Partnerships t-matters-for-educators-to-work-with-the-sutton-trust/
author: Sean Harris
summary: Sean Harris of Tees Valley Education argues that the main barrier facing young people in disadvantaged areas is rarely aspiration or effort but the uneven distribution of opportunity. Drawing on the Sutton Trust's Opportunity Index and a JRF report identifying 686 neighbourhoods with a double disadvantage of deprivation and weak social infrastructure, he says place shapes the menu from which choices are made. He urges educators to ask what an opportunity looked like from where a young person stood, and to make opportunity visible by widening the field of vision rather than importing ambition. Schools cannot compensate for every inequality, he says, but they remain among the few universal institutions and can act as civic anchors that convene partners instead of trying to be the heart of the community. Tees Valley Education's PLACE strategy teaches that schools do best when they ask who else cares about a problem. He closes by redefining opportunity as the signposting, the people and the transport that get a young person there.
points: Harris shifts the question from why a young person did not take an opportunity to what the opportunity looked like from where they were standing.
JRF research identifies 686 neighbourhoods, home to 5.7 million people, with high deprivation and weak social infrastructure, which makes identical incomes feel different in different places.
Disadvantaged children rarely lack dreams but often lack visibility of options, so making opportunity visible means widening the field of vision rather than raising aspiration.
He cautions against the rhetoric that schools are the beating heart of communities and prefers the idea of schools as civic anchors that convene and connect others.
The PLACE strategy suggests schools do their most impactful work when they ask who else cares about a problem and build an ecosystem with employers, charities, health partners and families.
quotes: Instead of asking, “Why didn’t this child or young person take the opportunity?”, perhaps we should ask, “What did the opportunity look like from where they were standing?

Researchers at JRF identify 686 neighbourhoods, home to 5.7 million people, facing what it describes as a “double disadvantage”, high levels of socioeconomic deprivation combined with weaker social infrastructure.
The income may look similar on a spreadsheet but the lived experience can be very different.

Children, young people and families do, of course, make choices. But choices are made and consequences are felt within different contexts and conditions, and place shapes the menu from which choices are understood and made.

The problem is not that disadvantaged children somehow lack dreams, but often they lack visibility and opportunity. It is difficult for a young person to choose something that they do not know exists.
Making opportunity visible is not about raising aspiration as though ambition needs importing into communities from elsewhere – it is about widening the field of vision.
Instead, this work means recognising their potential role as civic anchors; places which can convene, connect, and help strengthen the wider social infrastructure surrounding children and families.
Opportunity is a very tangible experience for a young person. It is the the place where it is signposted, the people that help them understand it, and the transport that gets them there.
